clinicalPearls: A distinctive intellectual disability syndrome with sparse scalp hair and prominent interphalangeal joints
The fingers show prominent, thickened interphalangeal joints and distal phalanges, often becoming more evident with age
Facial features include a triangular face, sparse hair, a wide mouth with a thin upper lip and thick lower lip
Seizures are common and can be difficult to control, and severe speech impairment is typical
Short stature and a friendly but sometimes irritable behavioural profile are described
Caused by de novo heterozygous variants in SMARCA2, a component of the BAF (SWI/SNF) chromatin-remodelling complex, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
The combination of sparse hair, distinctive digits and intellectual disability is highly suggestive
reference.pathophysiology: SMARCA2 encodes BRM, an ATPase subunit of the BAF (SWI/SNF) chromatin-remodelling complex, which uses ATP to reposition nucleosomes and thereby regulate access to DNA for transcription during development. Missense variants, typically de novo, alter the ATPase function and act through a dominant mechanism, dysregulating the expression of genes needed for normal brain, skin appendage and skeletal development. The disturbed chromatin remodelling produces the intellectual disability, epilepsy, sparse hair and characteristic digital and facial features. As a chromatin-remodelling disorder, it belongs to the broader group of BAF-complex (SWI/SNF) developmental syndromes that overlaps with Coffin-Siris syndrome.
additionalInvestigations: Hand and skeletal radiographs for prominent interphalangeal joints and phalangeal changes
EEG and brain MRI when seizures occur
Chromosomal microarray to exclude copy-number causes
Gene panel or exome sequencing including SMARCA2 and other BAF-complex genes
reference.prognosis: Nicolaides-Baraitser syndrome causes moderate to severe lifelong intellectual disability with limited speech; epilepsy severity is a major determinant of outcome. Care is supportive, with attention to seizures, development and orthopaedic features.
pitfalls: Mislabelling as an ectodermal dysplasia based on the sparse hair alone
Confusing it with Coffin-Siris syndrome without gene-level testing
Underestimating the severity and drug resistance of the epilepsy
Overlooking the progressive nature of the digital joint changes in young children
management: Provide supportive, symptom-directed care as there is no disease-modifying therapy for this chromatin-remodelling disorder
Control seizures with antiepileptic drugs, recognising that epilepsy is often difficult to treat and may need combination regimens

Deliver early developmental support with speech and language therapy, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and tailored special educational provision for the severe speech impairment and intellectual disability
Assess and manage the hand and skeletal features through orthopaedic and hand-therapy input
Monitor growth and nutrition given short stature, and offer behavioural support for the irritable behavioural profile
Coordinate multidisciplinary follow-up across clinical genetics, paediatric neurology and paediatrics
Provide genetic counselling, noting most cases arise from de novo SMARCA2 variants with a low recurrence risk in autosomal dominant inheritance
